comments.text:
My solution to the controversy.
1) No, AI art will never take the job of artists fully. Rather,  artists will adapt to use AI in their own way. And a simple prompt user will definitely loose to a person who combines their advances knowledge and technique PLUS advanced knowledge of AI and prompt-engeneering techniques  making it even better. As in, what would originally be a 90%-100% success without AI be turned into 100%- 110%. Those are the people I think that are the future of art, and it's those people I refer to when saying AI art can be good.
2).  No, this is not stealing. At least, if we use an official definition of stealing, this is much closer to a different version of what we call creativity. That said, there is a possibility of accidental plagiarism,  when the picture is obviously based on a specific work, but that can be easily resolved by just performing research before posting your image and redoing it. 
3) We can make AI not the whole process, but only the parts of it that we choose. Like, if I'm making a webseries, I can make  a soundtrack, a story, the dialogues, the world building myself, and use AI for voiceover. 
That being said, I myself do not usually post AI arts, unless  I specifically mention it's completely AI, simply because I am not the kind of artist I was referring to in the previous point (although I hope to be one day)

Look at the two faces. One is a blank stare. Nice to look at but there’s nothing in those eyes. One has a very decisive emotion behind it that is easy to relate to.

Art is not about creating beautiful things. Art often does result in beautiful things though because of what it actually is. It’s a means of human connection. It’s a form of communication between ourselves to display visceral ideas that we ourselves can’t be put any other way.

If art simply was just a means of creating “good images”, then yeah, sure. AI has “solved” art. We don’t need it anymore.

AI may be able to recreate the “ghibli style” or make hyper realistic images or have incredible shading, but it can’t conceive and invent something like Picasso’s Guernica, or the emotional weight of something like a Rothko painting. AI couldn’t think of signing a toilet and calling it art.

Dare I say, AI couldn’t think of something like taping a banana to a wall with duct tape.

Why?

Because these statements are windows into the minds of their creator.

Humans depend on connection. We need each other. Left on our own, we can not survive. We’re social creatures, introverted as some of us are. Art is a means of true human connection.

An AI could maybe write a really catchy melody. Four AI bots, however, couldn’t hang around each other in Liverpool, dreaming up romantic songs about their young lives in the 60s and express their joy to the world in the way they did. An AI might be able to write some surreal imagery and put it to an acoustic guitar. But it can’t pull together the experience and the single creative vision behind something by Bob Dylan. Heck, AI could ABSOLUTELY randomize white noise for 2 hours. But it can’t do it with the intentionality and the natural, human ebbing and flowing of someone like Merzbow. It can take a bunch of old records and maybe sorta cobble it together into an audio piece about dementia. But it couldn’t have the human heartbreak and empathy to create something like those final few minutes of The Caretaker’s EATEOT (which I think I’ve only heard 2 seconds of… but oh man, those 2 seconds…).

AI could end a cartoon episode about a fear of the outdoors in a silly way. But it takes a uniquely strange and funny group of people to end it with a guy in a gorilla suit literally smacking a wooden chair wwe style into an animated starfish and squirrel SUPPOSEDLY “in a bag” and then immediately stop when the talking sponge asks what the heck it’s doing underwater with a reveal that a family was watching the episode on TV in utter bewilderment.

It’s why when you talking about reading someone’s books or poems, you often refer to them as reading T.S. Elliott. You’re reading Dickinson. You’re reading Kafka. You’re reading Tolkien. You’re reading THEM. That’s what you’re there to read. Not in a parasocial way (hopefully), but in a way that you emotionally engage with their thoughts. You’re not there for the book itself: the collection of words in and of themselves.

AI, in this instance, only knows how to write the book.

Look, i love new technologies as much as the next guy. I consider myself a tech enthusiast and etc. 
But... Recently I went through a long journey on research and critical thinking to come to myself with the answer and proper arguments if "AI art" is real art. 
I'm a photographer and I take some pretty good pictures. But I don't consider my work or myself an artist. 
I embarked in this journey because sometimes it's pretty easy for us to just be bias against new things, to act with prejudice and etc. I started it pretty neutral but... 
When I went to some online forums of "Defending AI Art" or anything like that, I saw a lot o people whit passionate arguments and discussions of AI being able or not to make art. But, you know what I couldn't see? Yeah, ART. 
In the end, what I saw was a bunch of dudes whit AI made ANIME GIRLS holding signs saying "AI ART IS ART"... 
Like, dudes art reference is HATSUME MIKO? REALLY? 
There are some outstanding AI art-like works like "Théâtre D'opéra Spatial" and etc. 
But what we usually see is a bunch of lazy ass midlife crisis dudes with some kind of self confidence problems finding excuses to call themselves "artists"...
Honey, I know you probably had a absentee father or something like it and now you are starving for a feeling of validation (and honestly, so did I)... But if you are looking for validation in the field or art, I hate to be the bearer of bad news... 

Plus, we should use AI to do things that we don't want like going through a long spreadsheet or some boring task like that... 
Even if AI could make art... We, humans, don't do art because it had to be done or something, we do because we have this urge of expressing our feelings in a not very common way. We do because we like doing. We enjoy not only the final product but the process we take to come to that. We learn in the process. We learn about the technics we are using, the medium, we learn about ourselves and the feeling we are trying to deliver to our piece... And with AI there's no process. It's a prompt and then you have the final product.

I'm at minute 8, and I'm pausing the video to share with you a few thoughts about that first section.

I agree with your conclusions, I want to get that out of the way.

I'm a computer scientist with a background in research. I'm only saying that because I need to clarify a few points:

Machine Learning is a branch of Artificial Intelligence. LLMs are considered IA.

That doesn't mean LLMs are self aware, they're not, actually your explanation of how they work is very good. LLMs are probability churning machines.

AI doesn't necessarily implies Human-Like intelligence. There's a branch of AI that concerns in bio-inspired intelligence (machines that think like living things do) and LLMs are a form of that (deep neural networks).

But those models have limitations, and are not self-aware and don't fit the definition for creativity, no IA model does.

IA does exists, and machine learning is IA. IA is broader than Human-Like Intelligence, that doesn't exist yet and we are not sure if it will ever exist.

I would argue that specifically because the "AI" in AI art isnt actual AI, and there isnt any real intelligence behind it, is why it doesnt qualify as art.

What makes art "art" are the ideas behind them, the creativity of the mind, the intelligence if you will, that produced it. This requires at least some level of conscious intelligent input, or it does not count as art.

Everything else, from the technical skill to the aesthetic value to the practical or monetary value we normally associate with art is arbitrary, and thus secondary in my opinion, the thought behind art is what makes it art.
That is why a three year old's scrabbles of their stick figure parent with their eye level height house under a smiling sun is art, while a photocopy of the Mona Lisa is not.
And notably, this sets it completely apatt from pretty much every single function we  use actual art for in our current day society. It is another attempt at stripping the art from yet another part of the human experience.

So in short, the very fact that the "AI" behind "AI art" isnt really an AI, is what makes the "art" of "AI art" not real art.
